papers.title: A mitochondria-targeted ratiometric fluorescent probe for visualizing NO generation coupled with mitochondrial pH variations during autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper describes a new fluorescent probe designed to target mitochondria and simultaneously detect nitric oxide (NO) production and pH changes inside mitochondria. The probe uses a ratiometric fluorescence approach, meaning it measures the ratio of two signal intensities to give more reliable, quantitative readings. The tool is applied to study how NO generation and mitochondrial pH shift together during autophagy, the cellular process of degrading and recycling damaged components.
papers.why: This chemical probe offers a potential tool for directly visualizing mitochondrial pH and NO dynamics during mitophagy, which could be adapted to study mitochondrial quality control in neurons within the brain.
papers.figure: The figure showing time-course ratiometric fluorescence imaging of cells during autophagy induction, correlating NO signal changes with mitochondrial pH shifts.

papers.title: Metabolic regulation of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) homeostasis.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how cellular metabolism influences the maintenance, replication, and quality control of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). It likely covers how nutrient availability, metabolites, and energy sensing pathways affect mtDNA copy number, mutation load, and turnover. Understanding these regulatory mechanisms is central to how mitochondria adapt their genome to cellular metabolic demands and stress conditions.
papers.why: Since mitophagy is the primary quality-control mechanism for clearing damaged mitochondria and their DNA, insights into metabolic regulation of mtDNA homeostasis could inform how neuronal metabolic states and spatial metabolomic signatures relate to mitophagy activity in interneurons.

papers.title: EISCA and EISTA: Full-Spectrum Pipelines for Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics Analysis
papers.summary: EISCA and EISTA are described as comprehensive computational pipelines designed to analyze single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data, respectively. They likely cover the full workflow from raw data processing through quality control, normalization, clustering, and downstream biological interpretation. These tools aim to streamline and standardize analysis for researchers working with these increasingly common data types.
papers.why: Given the project's heavy reliance on spatial transcriptomics for studying interneurons and perineuronal nets, a dedicated full-spectrum analysis pipeline could substantially improve data processing efficiency and reproducibility.

papers.title: Inhibition of METTL14 Alleviates OGD/R-Induced Neuronal Differentiation Injury in Neural Stem Cells Through Suppressing the Tp53inp2/Ptgs2 Axis: Potential Benefits for the Mouse MCAO Model.
papers.summary: This study looked at how METTL14, an enzyme involved in m6A RNA modification, affects the ability of neural stem cells to develop into neurons after oxygen-glucose deprivation and reperfusion (OGD/R), a lab model mimicking stroke. The researchers found that blocking METTL14 improved neuronal differentiation by reducing the activity of a molecular pathway involving Tp53inp2 and Ptgs2. These benefits were also observed in a mouse stroke model (MCAO), suggesting METTL14 inhibition could help brain recovery after ischemic injury.
papers.why: Since Tp53inp2 is a known regulator of autophagy, this paper's findings on METTL14 suppressing the Tp53inp2/Ptgs2 axis could offer mechanistic insight into autophagy regulation in neuronal injury and recovery, relevant to the project's focus on mitophagy/autophagy in neurons.

papers.title: Autophagy determines the fate of immune cells by regulating metabolic remodeling and PANoptosis (Review).
papers.summary: This review discusses how autophagy influences the survival, differentiation, and death of immune cells by controlling their metabolic reprogramming. It also covers PANoptosis, a form of inflammatory cell death combining pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis features, and how autophagy regulates this process. The paper synthesizes current knowledge on the molecular links between autophagy, metabolism, and immune cell fate decisions.
papers.why: Although focused on immune cells rather than neurons, this review's mechanistic insights into autophagy-driven metabolic remodeling and cell fate regulation could inform how similar autophagy-metabolism crosstalk shapes neuronal and glial states relevant to mitophagy research in the brain.
papers.figure: A schematic diagram illustrating the molecular crosstalk between autophagy pathways, metabolic remodeling, and PANoptosis in immune cell fate decisions.

papers.title: Ultrastructural remodeling of mitochondria-associated vesicular structures in the rat medial prefrontal cortex following Propionic acid exposure.
papers.summary: This study looks at how exposure to propionic acid, a short-chain fatty acid linked to gut-brain axis research and autism models, changes the fine structural appearance of mitochondria and nearby small vesicle-like structures in the rat prefrontal cortex. Using electron microscopy, the researchers document alterations in mitochondrial shape and associated vesicular compartments, suggesting disrupted organelle quality control. These findings point to propionic acid as a trigger for mitochondrial stress and altered membrane trafficking in cortical neurons.
papers.why: This work provides ultrastructural evidence of mitochondria-associated vesicular remodeling potentially reflecting altered mitophagy/autophagy pathways in neurons, directly relevant to the project's focus on mitochondrial quality control in the brain.
papers.figure: Representative electron micrographs comparing mitochondrial and vesicular ultrastructure in control versus propionic acid-exposed prefrontal cortex neurons.

papers.title: Decoding cell-cell communication in spatial transcriptomics: mechanistic insights, modeling constraints, and analytical caveats.
papers.summary: This paper discusses methods and challenges in inferring cell-cell communication from spatial transcriptomics data. It covers the biological mechanisms behind signaling interactions, the modeling assumptions researchers make, and common pitfalls in current analytical pipelines. The goal is to help researchers more accurately interpret which cells are 'talking' to each other based on spatial gene expression patterns.
papers.why: Understanding cell-cell communication methods is directly relevant to analyzing spatial transcriptomics data on interneurons and perineuronal nets in the brain, since interactions between neurons and their extracellular matrix likely involve signaling that these computational tools aim to decode.

papers.title: ACSL5 drives pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by suppressing mitophagy and enhancing ferroptosis resistance via the JAK1-STAT1-OASL axis.
papers.summary: This paper studies ACSL5, a lipid metabolism enzyme, and shows it promotes pancreatic cancer growth by blocking mitophagy, a process that clears damaged mitochondria. ACSL5 also helps cancer cells resist ferroptosis, a form of iron-dependent cell death, by activating a signaling pathway involving JAK1, STAT1, and OASL. Together, these mechanisms allow pancreatic tumor cells to survive and evade cell death, making ACSL5 a potential therapeutic target.
papers.why: Although this paper focuses on pancreatic cancer rather than neurons, its detailed mechanistic insights into mitophagy suppression and its regulatory pathways could offer transferable concepts for understanding mitophagy dysregulation in neuronal contexts.
